body.text:
BZ clock for class demo. Want colour flips every ~60 s +/- 10 s, can I trust the 2-variable model?
NaBrO3 0.06 M (sodium bromate concentration)
malonic acid 0.02 M (malonic acid concentration)
H2SO4 -> [H+] 0.8 M (acid condition for hydrogen ion concentration)
catalyst: Ce(IV), stirred, 25 C (catalyst and reaction conditions)
~ 60 s +/- 10 s (desired colour flip period)

nodes.title: Full chemistry oscillates
nodes.statement: The full three-variable Oregonator with this recipe sustains repeating oscillations.
nodes.rationale: Without sustained oscillation in the full model there is no repeating clock to compare to a 60 s target.

check.description: Stiff Oregonator integration decides sustained oscillation for the stated recipe.
check.question: oscillates

nodes.title: Period hits classroom target
nodes.statement: The full oscillation cycle, which is what is seen as repeating colour flips, lasts about 60 seconds within 10 seconds.
nodes.rationale: The demo goal is explicit: the repeating colour-flip cycle should be about 60 seconds within 10 seconds.

check.description: Computed full-cycle time in seconds is compared with the 60 s classroom target.

nodes.title: Reduced model still oscillates
nodes.statement: The two-variable reduction still oscillates at this recipe rather than damping out.
nodes.rationale: A two-variable model that settles to steady state cannot be trusted for timing even if the full system oscillates.

check.description: Stiff Oregonator integration decides whether the reduced model still oscillates.
check.question: reduced_oscillates

nodes.title: Reduction preserves timing
nodes.statement: The two-variable reduction keeps essentially the same cycle time as the full model.
nodes.rationale: Trust in the simpler model for classroom timing rests on it preserving the cycle time, not just oscillating.

check.description: Engine compares full and reduced dimensionless periods for this recipe.
check.question: reduction_keeps_period

nodes.title: Mixing and catalyst apply
nodes.statement: Stirring keeps the beaker uniform and the cerium catalyst follows the Oregonator kinetics at room temperature.
nodes.rationale: Oregonator rate constants and mapping assume well-mixed cerium-catalysed chemistry near 25 C; unstirred gradients or a different catalyst break it.

nodes.title: Demo is visible and safe
nodes.statement: Colour flips are clearly visible and the stirred acid bromate mixture can be run safely as a classroom demo.
nodes.rationale: Even with correct timing, a class demo needs visible colour contrast and safe handling of strong acid and bromate.

body.summary: Read as a stirred cerium-catalysed batch clock whose repeating colour-flip cycle should be ~60 s, not a single flip; main alternative would be an unmixed pattern-forming display where timing differs by location.

body.reason: With s=1 and small eps, very small q and eps_prime this recipe lies in the classic oscillatory regime of the Oregonator.
Very small eps_prime justifies y quasi-steady-state reduction and eps near 0.01 with tiny q and s=1 lies in the classic relaxation-oscillation regime.
eps_prime is ~500x smaller than eps, so the y quasi-steady-state separation is strong and period error should stay under 10%.

body.question: The clock misses the 60 s I want. What should I change in the recipe, and what would that risk?
body.answer: VIBloom computed that dimensional period is set by an inverse malonic-acid timescale. My reasoning is that raising malonic acid is the direct recipe lever to shorten the cycle. That risks losing timescale separation and stopping oscillation, so recheck oscillation validity after any change. Open classroom usability next to check visibility and safe handling before testing.

body.reason: Epsilon ~0.1 with very small q and very fast y is within the classic relaxation-oscillation regime for f/s ~1.
Very small q and eps_prime preserve excitability and eps near 0.1 is still below the typical Hopf damping boundary for s=1, so limit-cycle oscillation is expected.
eps_prime is ~500x smaller than eps so the fast-variable quasi-steady elimination is well separated and should preserve period within 10%.

candidates.explanation: The reduction shortens the oscillation period because eps is too large for the slow manifold to remain separated from the fast jump during the excited phase.
candidates.scope: Reductions where the slow timescale separation is incomplete while the fast variable remains well separated from the slow variables.

candidates.explanation: The reduction shortens the oscillation period because elimination of the fast variable shifts the excitation threshold controlled by small q and reshapes the nullcline intersection.
candidates.scope: Reductions where q remains far below unity so threshold geometry dominates period independent of slow timescale separation.

body.open: A single bromate comparison cannot establish the range of slow timescale separation over which the reduction preserves period.
